title: Adding an “artificial” star to the multitude in the sky
caption: A laser guide star beam from the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at Paranal Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: Published in the ESO image archive. No published rating.

story: Beneath trails left by stars on a dark, clear night, a laser beam shoots skyward from Yepun, the fourth Unit Telescope of ESO's Very Large Telescope. ESO calls the VLT Europe's flagship observatory.

The laser creates an artificial star above Paranal. Astronomers cannot always find a bright real star in just the right spot, so they make their own, and the VLT's adaptive optics instruments use it as a guide.

Adaptive optics is a way around the blurring caused by Earth's atmosphere. As starlight passes through moving layers of air, it gets smeared, which is why stars twinkle. By tracking how the artificial star is distorted, the system can measure the smearing and correct for it continuously. ESO says this produces images almost as sharp as they would be if the whole telescope were in space, above the atmosphere.

understand.summary: This is a long-exposure landscape photograph taken in visible light with a camera at Paranal. The exposure settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: The eye would see the stars as points of light. The trails appear only because the camera gathered light over a long time.

explore: The trails of the real stars behind the beam record Earth's rotation, which makes the sky appear to turn over the course of the night.
